newsitem.title: USA: Post hails last year's price cuts for sales boost.
newsitem.headline: Post hails last year's price cuts for sales boost.

text.p: A year after Post Cereal shook up the $9 billion ready-to-eat cereal industry by cutting prices 20 percent, the company hailed the move that boosted its sales volume faster than the industry.
"We've been very happy with the result," said Post Cereal General Manager Mark Leckie. "We wouldn't hesitate to do it again."

But others say industry price reductions -- after leader Kellogg Co. and second-place General Mills Inc. followed Post with smaller-scale cuts -- have not significantly picked up the pace of cereal sales growth.
The overall U.S. cereal market is growing by about 1.5 percent annually, below the historic trend of 3 percent, according to industry figures.
"It's possible that it would have been worse without the price cut. But the price cut did not meaningfully stimulate growth in the category," Goldman Sachs analyst Nomi Ghez said.
One reason, she added, is that many cereal makers reduced promotions and discounts when they cut prices. As a result, the net price to the consumer was not reduced dramatically.

But Post, with the broadest price cuts, saw its market share rise by 1.7 points to an average of 17.1 percent since the price roll-back, Leckie said. Post is a division of Kraft Foods Inc., which is part of Philip Morris Cos. Inc.
"This is a business (Post Cereal) that was losing share and declining in tonnage, and now it is growing faster than either Kellogg or General Mills in tonnage," Leckie added.

According to Information Resources, which tracks sales in grocery stores only, Post's cereal volume for the 52 weeks ended Feb. 23 rose 7.6 percent to 432.8 million pounds. Post's cereal brands include Grape Nuts and Post Premium Raisin Bran.

By comparison, Kellogg, which makes Corn Flakes and Rice Krispies, showed a 9 percent decline in sales to 830.6 million pounds for the 52-week period. General Mills, the maker of Wheaties and Cheerios, had a 1.1 percent rise in sales to 614 million pounds, Information Resources added.
While price cuts helped Post grab market share, for the overall industry the roll-back has not been enough.

"The price decrease didn't affect overall industry trends. What that says is you need news and innovation to drive growth," said Douglas Mills, executive vice president of U.S. and Canadian Foods for Quaker Oats Co. Quaker, the fourth largest U.S. cereal company with brands like Life and Cap'n Crunch, had a 1.7 percent increase in sales to 207.4 million pounds in the 52-week period.

Companies have stepped up the pace of new product roll-outs recently, with offerings such as Kellogg's Cocoa Frosted Flakes, Post's Cranberry Almond Crunch, and General Mills' Betty Crocker cereal line.
Looking ahead, the pace of cereal industry growth could quicken as new products attract attention and consumers are weaned from deep-discount promotions and coupons.

"Consumers have had to learn to buy cereal in a different fashion. The deep discounts of 1993 to 1995 are not there," CS First Boston analyst Michael Mauboussin said. "There is reason to be optimistic that unit volume growth of 2-3 percent may be reasonable."
